parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a fleet technician. You will interview each of the other roles separately.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- You can ask at most 30 questions in this interview.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.
Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from start to end?

I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order. I add new drones to our fleet, retire old ones, set up our charging pads at our sites, and take drones out of service for repairs and put them back. I also send drones to charge, and regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.
When you arrive in the morning, what is the very first thing you do, and how does the day usually unfold from there?
I don't know.
That's okay. Could you give me a concrete example of taking a drone out of service for repairs and putting it back—what triggers it, and what steps do you take?
I don't know.
Who hands work to you, and who do you hand work off to during your shifts?
I don't know.
Tell me about the worst working day you've had in the last few months—what happened and what made it bad?
I don't know.
What do you check by hand today because you don't fully trust the current tools or information?
I don't know.
Right after something goes wrong with a drone or a charging pad, what do you need to know first?
I don't know.
Thinking about a new shared service coming in, what are you afraid it might get wrong?
I don't know.
When regulators ask your company to show how your drones have been looked after, what exact information do you have to show them?
I don't know.
How do you decide when to send a drone to charge, and how does that work?

I send drones to charge, and I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order. I also add new drones to the fleet, retire old ones, set up charging pads at our sites, and take drones out of service for repairs and put them back.
What information matters when you add a new drone to the fleet or set up a charging pad at a site?

I add new drones to the fleet and set up charging pads at our sites as part of keeping our drones and charging equipment in working order. Our company has a few dozen charging pads at our own sites, and several connector types are in use that are not interchangeable. Each drone has a home site, and our drones come in several models from different manufacturers with different capabilities for carrying loads, flying distance, sensors, and charging connectors.
What needs to match or be available when you send a drone to a charging pad?

I send drones to charge, and several connector types are in use that are not interchangeable. Our company has its own charging pads at our own sites, a few dozen of them, and each drone has a home site.
Can a drone charge at any of your company's sites, or only at its home site?
Each drone has a home site, and our company has its own charging pads at our own sites, a few dozen of them. Several connector types are in use and they are not interchangeable.
How do the dispatchers or the airspace desk find out when you take a drone out of service, put it back, or retire it?
I don't know.
